segments.title: Confederate steam rams and Royal Navy purchase
segments.summary: The Battle of Lissa and the American Civil War made steam rams look important, while two Cammell Laird ships gave the Royal Navy a practical reason to test the idea.
segments.body: The Battle of Lissa and the American Civil War made steam rams look like an important new capability. Cammell Laird built these two vessels officially for Egypt and, in the account given here, unofficially for the Confederacy. The Royal Navy bought them to prevent them from becoming a problem. The extra ships extended the fleet's presence and allowed the service to test the technology. Those benefits said little about whether ramming was a useful primary weapon. The purchase shows how strategic denial and an opportunity to experiment could bring a doubtful design into service.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces steam rams, Lissa, and the American Civil War as examples that made ramming look important.
The transcript says the two vessels were built officially for Egypt, unofficially for the Confederacy, and force-purchased by the Royal Navy.
The transcript asks whether the Royal Navy received value from the ships, while noting the value of extra ships and technology testing.

segments.title: Why ancient ramming does not translate
segments.summary: A comparison with triremes shows why ramming made sense when ships closed for boarding, but became a bad primary weapon once guns and shells could sink ships at range.
segments.body: Ramming suited ancient galley combat because ships already had to close for boarding. A ram could damage the enemy before that contact, although the collision might also tear the ram from the attacker's hull. Steam-era warships carried guns and explosive shells that could sink an opponent without risking the same collision damage. If pointing the whole ship at a target was the only reliable way to hit it, the navy had failures in command, control, and training. A weapon suited to one tactical system became a liability once range, firepower, and fleet control changed.

evidence.note: The transcript says ramming as a primary weapon does not work, then explains why rams were principal weapons for Greek and Roman triremes.
The transcript links ancient ramming to boarding-range combat and warns that ramming could damage the attacker's own ship.
The transcript argues that steam-era ships had guns and explosive shells, and that needing to ram to hit a target points to command, control, and training failures.

segments.title: Ramming as secondary bow strength
segments.summary: A strengthened bow or emergency ramming ability could still be useful, but it did not justify building a warship around collision with another armored ship.
segments.body: By the time of Tsushima, the ram had returned to a secondary role rather than serving as a fleet's main tactic. A strengthened bow could still be useful in special cases, as HMS Dreadnought demonstrated when its only kill came from ramming a submarine. That success did not justify deliberately colliding with an equivalently armored battleship. A ramming melee at Jutland would also have ignored the torpedoes and long-range artillery available to both fleets. Age-of-sail prize warfare imposed another limit: a navy hoping to capture an enemy vessel gained nothing by sinking or crippling both ships in a collision.

evidence.note: The transcript says rams returned to a secondary role after Tsushima and cites HMS Dreadnought's submarine kill by ramming.
The transcript contrasts ramming at Jutland with torpedoes and long-range artillery, then says ramming an enemy ship also damages one's own.
The transcript says a navy that wants to capture ships does not want to ram them, then questions the return of rams in the steam and ironclad era.

segments.title: Ramming invites the enemy to cross the T
segments.summary: A ship charging bow-first to ram gives up much of its own broadside, lets the enemy cross its T, and invites concentrated gunfire.
segments.body: A ship charging to ram points its bow at the enemy while the target can concentrate more guns against it. This exposure recreates the familiar problem of letting the enemy cross the T. The attacker gives up much of its own broadside and follows a predictable approach under fire. Poor gunnery accuracy was a training and command problem, not a reason to replace gunfire with collision. The same ramming mindset helps explain the pre-dreadnought and dreadnought interest in heavy forward fire for a head-on approach.

evidence.note: The transcript says ramming lets the enemy cross the T because the target can concentrate guns while the rammer cannot.
The transcript links this problem to pre-dreadnought and dreadnought fixation on guns firing forward.
The transcript calls steam rams a bad idea for the Royal Navy and argues that ship-sized targets were visible enough at likely engagement ranges.

segments.title: Confined waters and luck at Lissa
segments.summary: Successful ramming depended on confined waters, limited maneuvering control, and luck, conditions that offered no sound basis for open-water doctrine.
segments.body: Ramming sometimes worked under conditions that were hard to reproduce. Civil War rivers and estuaries, along with the Adriatic setting of the Battle of Lissa, restricted maneuver and made avoidance more difficult. In open water, the attacker had to close through gunfire and often needed some degree of surprise. A target with room and control to turn could make the ram glance off or strike at a poor angle. Steam rams therefore belonged among schemes occasionally made successful by luck, not among dependable primary weapons.

evidence.note: The transcript says open-water ramming requires ambush and closing into gunfire, while Civil War and Lissa examples involved confined waters.
The transcript says a target should be able to turn so the ram glances off or reaches a poor angle.
The transcript places steam rams in the category of crackpot schemes occasionally well executed because of luck.
